questions.text: When designing small-unit tests for data cleaning functions, which assertion is most valuable to catch silent schema drift?
options: Assert function runs without exception
Assert that output contains expected column names and types
Assert execution time is below threshold

questions.correct_answer: Assert that output contains expected column names and types

questions.text: You are extracting customer name data from multiple sources. Some sources return "John Smith" while others return "smith, john". After combining data, you notice duplicate records that differ only in name format. Which approach best handles this situation?
options: Keep both formats since they contain same information
Normalize to first/last name components, standardize case/order, then deduplicate
Delete all records appearing as duplicates arbitrarily
Require users to manually resolve each formatting issue
questions.correct_answer: Normalize to first/last name components, standardize case/order, then deduplicate

questions.text: Your team uses an external weather API in automated tests. The API sometimes returns temporary errors (500 errors). Which testing approach is most reliable?
options: Test against live API every time, accept occasional 500 failures
Record real API responses as offline test files, use files normally, test live periodically
Skip API tests since provider handles reliability
Mock the API by hardcoding expected weather values for specific cities
questions.correct_answer: Record real API responses as offline test files, use files normally, test live periodically

questions.text: You are combining product data from two suppliers. Supplier A has product names like "Blue T- Shirt Size M" and Supplier B has "tshirt blue m". Why is it difficult to identify these as the same product using simple text matching?
options: The names include extra descriptive words that do not appear in both supplier listings.
Effective text comparison requires accounting for variations in word order, abbreviations, and synonyms, as a simple word-by-word match is insufficient.
Text matching is impossible with product names
The product codes are different so they must be different products
questions.correct_answer: Effective text comparison requires accounting for variations in word order, abbreviations, and synonyms, as a simple word-by-word match is insufficient.

questions.text: In a bash ETL script that runs on a schedule, what should you do to make sure the job can run repeatedly without causing bad or duplicated results (i.e., to keep it idempotent)?
options: Always write straight into the final output file and overwrite it every time
Write to temp file, atomic move to final, track processed records
Delete all output files at the start of every run
Run the job several times at once so at least one run succeeds
questions.correct_answer: Write to temp file, atomic move to final, track processed records

questions.text: When converting mixed-currency product feeds for analytics, why store original currency along with converted value?
options: It is redundant and unnecessary
Enables recalculation if exchange rates change later
It doubles storage but has no benefit
It makes queries faster
questions.correct_answer: Enables recalculation if exchange rates change later

questions.text: You maintain a Python script that cleans data. The script uses an external library (e.g., pandas) that your organization will support for the next 2 years. However, a new version of pandas is released with bug fixes. What is the best practice?
options: Immediately upgrade to the latest version of all dependencies
Document current version, test new version separately, upgrade if compatible
Never update any library since updates always break things
Remove the pandas dependency and rewrite your script without it
questions.correct_answer: Document current version, test new version separately, upgrade if compatible

questions.text: Your team develops an automated pipeline that classifies customer support tickets into categories. A team member used an AI assistant to write the classification code. The code works correctly in testing but occasionally produces unexpected categories in production. What is the best way to identify and fix this issue?
options: Remove the AI-generated code and rewrite it from scratch
Capture production failures as test cases, fix code, save tests permanently
Accept occasional errors as normal and monitor the error rate
Disable the AI assistant for the entire team
questions.correct_answer: Capture production failures as test cases, fix code, save tests permanently

questions.text: Which provenance strategy most reliably supports reproducing a processed dataset months later when upstream providers may change?
options: Only store final processed CSV
Archive raw inputs, code, dependency versions, artifact hashes in manifest
Rely on upstream to provide same data again
Keep only commit timestamps
questions.correct_answer: Archive raw inputs, code, dependency versions, artifact hashes in manifest

questions.text: For scaling interactive data cleaning to large datasets while retaining reproducibility and human review, the best architecture is:
options: Pure in-memory interactive tool for all rows
Sample-driven transforms as reusable ETL recipes with manual review flags
Manual spreadsheet edits for samples then manual application
Single-run interactive session exported as final CSV
questions.correct_answer: Sample-driven transforms as reusable ETL recipes with manual review flags

questions.text: When designing schema validation for heterogeneous JSON providers, the most robust rule set:
